nameStory: The green dragon gets its dramatic name from its unusual flower structure, which looks like a long, slender dragon's tail emerging from a green hood. Unlike its cousin jack-in-the-pulpit, where the spadix (the spike-like flower part) stays hidden inside the spathe (the hood), the green dragon's spadix extends well beyond its covering like a serpent's tail poking out of a cave.
description: Green dragon is a woodland wildflower that's like jack-in-the-pulpit's more dramatic cousin. This plant grows from an underground bulb-like corm and typically reaches 8-20 inches tall during blooming, though it can stretch to over 3 feet after flowering. What makes it instantly recognizable is its single, umbrella-like leaf divided into 7-13 narrow leaflets that spread out horizontally, and its distinctive spring flower with a long 'tail' that extends beyond its green hood.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: A slender green hood (spathe) covers the base of a long, thin, tail-like spike (spadix) that extends 2-6 inches beyond the hood, giving it the signature dragon-tail appearance in spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Single compound leaf with 7-13 narrow, pointed leaflets arranged like fingers spreading from a palm, with the center leaflet largest and outer ones getting progressively smaller

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Usually just one leaf per plant held horizontally like an umbrella, emerging from ground level with no visible stem above the soil surface

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Club-shaped cluster of berries that starts green in summer and turns bright orange-red by late summer, containing up to 150 individual berries

habitat: Green dragon prefers moist, rich woodland soils in deciduous or mixed forests, often found in the same damp, shady spots as jack-in-the-pulpit. Look for it in low-lying areas, along stream banks, and in forest hollows where the soil stays consistently moist. It's much less common than jack-in-the-pulpit throughout New England, with only scattered populations reported.

seasonality.spring: The distinctive dragon-tail flower appears in late spring, making this the best time for identification when the long spadix extends prominently from its green spathe hood.
seasonality.summer: The single umbrella-like leaf reaches full size and the developing fruit cluster begins to form where the flower was, still green and club-shaped.
seasonality.fall: The berry cluster ripens to bright orange-red, making it visible from a distance, while the leaf may begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely underground to its corm, leaving no visible trace above ground until the following spring.

funFact: In the 1830s, American travelers reported that some people used green dragon root (called 'dragon-root') as a primitive toothbrush, rubbing it directly on their teeth - though this practice would be quite painful since the plant contains sharp calcium oxalate crystals that can burn your mouth!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with jack-in-the-pulpit, but green dragon's long tail extending from the flower hood is unmistakable. Remember: if you see a dragon's tail poking out, it's green dragon; if the spike stays hidden inside the hood like a person in a pulpit, it's jack-in-the-pulpit.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the same genus as jack-in-the-pulpit, green dragon is much rarer and is actually listed as a vulnerable species in Canada. The entire Arisaema genus contains calcium oxalate crystals that make the plants very irritating to eat raw, though some Native American groups developed methods to process them safely.
compareHints: Green dragon differs from all its Arisaema relatives by having the spadix (flower spike) extend well beyond the spathe (hood), creating the characteristic tail. Jack-in-the-pulpit keeps its spadix hidden inside the striped spathe, while bog and small jack-in-the-pulpits also have enclosed spadixes. Green dragon also typically has more leaflets (7-13) compared to jack-in-the-pulpit's usual three leaflets.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Jack-in-the-pulpit is the most common of its relatives in New England, distinguished from green dragon by having just 1-2 three-part leaves (green dragon has one leaf with 5-15 leaflets).
Compared to common Jack-in-the-pulpit, bog Jack-in-the-pulpit is noticeably smaller and more delicate, preferring wet boggy conditions over typical woodland floors.
Compared to regular Jack-in-the-pulpit, small Jack is dramatically smaller in all aspects and prefers wetter habitats.
